This could be a critical factor for customers weighing the decision to switch to dynamic pricing, as the potential reduction in their overall energy costs could be diminished by these non-volumetric components of their bill. Understanding how these different tariff elements interact is important for assessing the true financial incentives of dynamic pricing schemes. Additionally, while the study forecasted dynamic prices to 2030, it lacks baseline time-of-use (TOU) rates for that future scenario. While these alternative rates aren’t particularly relevant for modeling price response behaviors and values, they greatly impact customers’ choice to adopt the dynamic tariff. Having a baseline of more common TOU rates would provide the ability to assess the bill impacts not only of customers responding to a dynamic price, but of them switching and responding to the rate. In future work, it will be essential to model a wider variety of realistic tariff designs and to assess how features like fixed charges and demand charges impact both customer behavior and overall bill savings. Expanding the scope of tariff structures will lead to more accurate predictions of customer adoption rates and will help to better understand the full economic impact of switching to dynamic tariffs. 4.5.3 End use response models The end use load response models developed for this study have certain limitations, each of which is detailed in the relevant subsection of Section 2.3. Future work should address these limitations by calibrating model results to ongoing pilots and demonstrations, ensuring that real- world data informs the accuracy of model predictions. Additionally, there is a need to consider more behavioral factors and potential limitations to flexibility settings, as customer behavior can significantly impact load response. Each end use category may have unique flexibility constraints and response strategies that were not fully captured in this study, necessitating further refinement of the models. 64 While the study focused on key end uses, many end uses were not covered. The thermal load shift model, for example, could potentially be expanded to capture shifts in refrigeration loads with the development of appropriate parameters. Future research should also focus on developing new response models for additional end uses that have flexibility potential, such as industrial facilities, water pumping loads (beyond crop irrigation), and residential appliances like washing machines, dryers, and dishwashers. These categories represent significant opportunities for load flexibility that were not modeled in this study but could contribute to more comprehensive demand response strategies. Regarding electric vehicle (EV) load shifting, the model applied in this study was limited by its focus on residential charging loads. While the model is adaptable, its scope in the current study did not extend to workplace charging due to complexities in the underlying load model data. While much of this commercial EV load already occurs during the day—when dynamic price signals may be less impactful—the exclusion of non-residential EV load leaves a gap in assessing the full price response potential of EVs.
